items.title: AI enthusiasts are in a race against time, AI skeptics are in a race against entropy
items.summary: Charity Majors argues both sides of the AI productivity debate are right but disconnected — enthusiasts have real, non-imaginary productivity leaps; skeptics are right that shipping code faster than teams can read it quietly depletes reliability and institutional knowledge. The trouble is there's no feedback loop between the two camps. A rare piece that validates both perspectives without being wishy-washy about it.

items.title: Programming (with AI agents) as theory building
items.summary: Riffs on Peter Naur's 1985 idea that the real output of programming is the programmer's mental model of the system, not the code itself. With AI agents writing more code, engineers build coarser theories — and Goedecke argues that's the tradeoff, and it's fine. Also takes on whether AI can build a "theory" of a codebase: pragmatically, if it can correctly answer questions and test hypotheses, the distinction stops mattering.

items.title: Are Memories Transferable — or Edible?
items.summary: In the 1960s, James McConnell trained flatworms to cringe at light, then fed trained-worm paste to untrained worms — which then learned faster, as if they'd eaten the memory. The claim was laughed out of mainstream neuroscience. Now a Harvard lab is revisiting it. Claire L. Evans traces the strange history and the scientists who can't quite let go of the question.

items.title: How I use LLMs as a staff engineer in 2026
items.summary: An honest practical update from a GitHub staff engineer on a year's worth of LLM workflow evolution — now producing entire PRs in familiar codebases, throwing every bug at an agent first (it correctly diagnoses ~80%), and running dozens of agent sessions a day. What makes it worth reading is the specificity: not 'LLMs are great,' but exactly where they took over and what that changed about the work.

items.title: The Feedback Loop Hypothesis: why agents find databases easy and websites hard
items.summary: Brooker argues the real limit on coding agents isn't raw model smarts but feedback: they thrive where it's fast and automatable (compilers, tests, formal specs) and flounder where it's "slow, squishy, and inconsistent" (UI, architecture). The counterintuitive payoff — system software is "easy", SaaS is "hard" — reframes the actual engineering work as building better feedback loops, not better prompts.

items.title: How coding agents actually work
items.summary: A clear, demystifying walk through what a coding agent really is: a harness around an LLM — system prompt, a tool-calling loop, token mechanics — that you could build yourself in a few dozen lines. Part of Willison's Agentic Engineering Patterns series, and the best antidote to treating agents as magic.

items.title: You don't know HTML Lists
items.summary: A surprisingly deep tour of all five HTML list types and when each is semantically right — the gist being that ordered lists are about sequence-that-matters, not numbering, and you've probably been reaching for the wrong one. Nerdy in the best way, and genuinely useful for accessibility.

items.title: Reality has a surprising amount of detail
items.summary: A classic essay worth (re)reading: every task — building stairs, boiling water — hides far more meaningful detail than you expect, and those details turn invisible once mastered, quietly stalling your learning. A small idea that changes how you look at any hard problem.
